topic_and_scope: A narrative synthesis of how microbiome alterations across gut, oral, and ocular sites may influence uveitis pathogenesis, the evidence from animal and human studies, and the potential and challenges of microbiome-targeted therapies in uveitis management and prevention.
main_themes: Mechanistic links between microbiome alterations and uveitis (antigen mimicry, barrier integrity, anti-inflammatory metabolite production, and systemic immune modulation)
Microbiome alterations across systemic diseases associated with uveitis and their diagnostic/therapeutic implications
Therapeutic modulation of the microbiome (probiotics, prebiotics, antibiotics, FMT, and immunomodulatory drugs) and the need for rigorous human trials and safety data
main_findings: Evidence supports four main microbiome-driven mechanisms in autoimmune uveitis: antigen mimicry, loss of intestinal immune homeostasis with a Th17/Treg imbalance, reduced anti-inflammatory microbial metabolites (notably short-chain fatty acids), and impaired intestinal barrier integrity leading to systemic inflammatory signals reaching the eye.

Animal model data show that altering the microbiome (via antibiotics or SCFA administration) can attenuate or exacerbate uveitis, indicating microbiome composition actively modulates disease severity and immune responses.

Human data reveal dysbiosis in uveitis patients and in systemic diseases associated with uveitis (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, Behçet’s disease), but causality remains unproven due to cross-sectional designs and confounding factors.

Therapeutic approaches targeting the microbiome (probiotics/prebiotics, antibiotics, FMT, and immunomodulatory drugs) show preclinical promise but lack robust, large-scale clinical trials in uveitis and have unclear safety/efficacy profiles in humans.

key_gaps.description: Specific microbial antigens driving autoimmune uveitis in humans have not been identified; causal roles and cross-reactive epitopes remain speculative based on animal and associative human data.

There is a lack of human clinical trials verifying the safety and efficacy of microbiome-based therapies (especially FMT) in uveitis, and standardized methodologies to study the microbiome in this disease are not established.

future_directions.title: Identify human microbial antigens driving autoimmune uveitis and validate cross-reactive T cell responses
future_directions.rationale: The review highlights a critical gap in identifying specific microbial triggers. A multifaceted approach combining metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, proteomics, and T cell epitope mapping should be used on samples from patients with non-infectious uveitis and suitable controls. In vitro assays to test cross-reactivity between gut/oral/mocular microbial peptides and retinal antigens, followed by in vivo validation in susceptible animal models (EAU), could establish causality and reveal candidate mimotopes for targeted therapies or tolerance induction.

future_directions.title: Launch large, multi-center longitudinal cohorts to map microbiome dynamics before and during uveitis flares
future_directions.rationale: Causality remains unproven due to cross-sectional human data. Prospective cohorts across uveitis subtypes and systemic diseases should collect serial gut, oral, and ocular microbiome samples, along with immune profiling and clinical outcomes. Advanced causal inference, time-series analyses, and machine learning should identify dysbiosis signatures that predict onset or relapse, enabling preventative microbiome-targeted interventions.

future_directions.title: Develop standardized, cross-study microbiome methodologies for uveitis research
future_directions.rationale: The field currently lacks standardized protocols, hindering reproducibility and comparability. Establish consensus guidelines for sampling (gastrointestinal, oral, ocular surfaces and intraocular fluids), sequencing platforms (16S, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics), data processing pipelines, and reporting metrics. Create an open, centralized data repository with harmonized metadata to enable meta-analyses and reproducible findings.

future_directions.title: Conduct randomized controlled trials of targeted probiotics and prebiotics in non-infectious uveitis
future_directions.rationale: Preclinical data show benefits from specific probiotic mixtures and SCFA supplementation. Rigorous human trials should define optimal strains, dosages, and durations, with endpoints including anterior/posterior segment inflammation scores, steroid-sparing effects, quality of life, and safety. Stratify by uveitis subtype and concomitant immunosuppressive therapies to determine responsive subgroups.

future_directions.title: Evaluate short-chain fatty acid supplementation as an adjunct therapy in uveitis
future_directions.rationale: SCFAs like propionate and butyrate reduced disease severity in animal models by promoting regulatory T cells and reinforcing barrier function. Early-phase human studies should assess tolerability, dosing, and biomarkers (Treg frequency, intestinal/blood permeability markers, ocular inflammatory indices). If safe, progress to larger efficacy trials, including combination regimens with standard immunosuppressants.

future_directions.title: Systematically assess fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) safety and efficacy for uveitis in controlled trials
future_directions.rationale: Animal data show context-dependent effects of microbiome transplantation on uveitis; no human trials exist. Phased clinical research is needed, starting with carefully screened donors, defined recipient populations (by subtype and systemic disease), and rigorous safety monitoring. Parallel microbiome engraftment assessments (metagenomics, metabolomics) and ocular outcome tracking should be integrated to identify beneficial vs. detrimental donor profiles.

future_directions.title: Elucidate mechanisms and therapeutic targets to strengthen gut barrier and limit ocular inflammation
future_directions.rationale: Increased intestinal permeability correlates with earlier onset and greater severity of uveitis. Mechanistic studies should test barrier-enhancing strategies (e.g., modulators of tight junctions, mucus layer integrity, or mucosal immunity) in EAU models and translate promising approaches to early-phase human trials. Biomarkers of barrier function (zonulin, LPS, tight junction proteins) should accompany clinical assessments to guide therapy.
